title: Miles Davis Was Born 100 Years Ago — and He Changed Music Over and Over Again!
summary: What if an artist could change their style so many times that each new album felt like a different person? That's what Miles Davis did. Born 100 years ago on May 26, 1926, he was a trumpet player who never stopped experimenting. He started in the fast, tricky style called bebop, then invented a cooler, calmer sound. His album Kind of Blue is the most popular jazz album in history — it's like the Harry Potter of jazz, a book everyone has read. But Miles didn't stop there. In the 1970s, he plugged in electric instruments and mixed jazz with rock and funk, making an album called Bitches Brew that blew people's minds. He was always pushing forward, even when it confused his fans. To celebrate his 100th birthday, a radio station in Philadelphia is playing his music for 24 hours straight! There are also special podcast episodes that explain his life and his most famous album. Miles Davis once said, "Don't play what's there, play what's not there." He meant that the best music comes from taking risks and trying new things. So put on some headphones and listen — you might just discover a whole new world of sound.
why_it_matters: Miles Davis proves that you don't have to stick to one style your whole life — trying new things, even if others get confused, can lead to brilliant discoveries.

background_read: Miles Davis (a trumpet player born in 1926) is one of the most important names in all of music, not just jazz.
Jazz began in New Orleans over 100 years ago, and it has changed many times — bebop was one wild, fast chapter of that story.
The album Kind of Blue, released in 1959, is still bought and streamed millions of times today, even by people who don't usually listen to jazz.
Article_Structure: WHO: Miles Davis, a trumpet player who kept reinventing jazz.
WHAT: He moved from bebop to cool jazz, then surprised everyone with electric sound on Bitches Brew, and his 100th birthday is being celebrated with a 24-hour radio special.
WHERE: His career was worldwide, but the article mentions a radio station in Philadelphia giving a special tribute.
WHY: To show how one artist never stopped experimenting and taking risks, leaving behind music that still excites new generations.

perspectives.description: Many fans and musicians call him a genius because he kept inventing fresh sounds and wasn't afraid to break the rules.
When he embraced loud electric music, some older jazz lovers felt he had left behind the beautiful sound they loved.
Looking back, each of his big changes later inspired whole new types of music, showing that being restless can reshape an art form.
